# Dependencies {#sec-dependencies}

Few applications are built from their own code alone. This chapter is about getting other
people's code into your build, the same way on every platform.

## Three ways to get dependencies {#sec-dependency-families}

Every approach belongs to one of three families.

| Family | Tools | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| Package managers | vcpkg, Conan | you have several dependencies, several platforms, and want prebuilt binaries cached |
| CMake-native | `FetchContent`, CPM.cmake, `find_package` with system packages | you have a few small dependencies, or target one platform whose packages you trust |
| Source-level | copying the code in ("vendoring"), git submodules or subtrees | you patch the dependency, or develop it alongside your app |

**Package manager:**

```{.json filename="vcpkg.json"}
{
  "dependencies": ["catch2", "glaze"]
}
```

**CMake-native:**

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
include(FetchContent)
FetchContent_Declare(fmt
    GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt.git
    GIT_TAG 11.2.0
)
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt)
```

**Source-level:**

```sh
git submodule add https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt.git external/fmt
```

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
add_subdirectory(external/fmt)
```

Source-level integration is common and often the right call. When you carry your own
patches, or change a library as often as your app, having its code in your tree is the most
flexible setup. The price: you update it by hand, and it builds with your project every
time.

Package managers sit at the other end. They resolve versions, build each library once and
cache the result, and work the same on every platform. The more dependencies and platforms
you have, the more that pays.

## `find_package` is the stable interface {#sec-find-package}

Whichever package manager or system provides a dependency, consume it the same way:
`find_package()` plus the imported target it defines.

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
find_package(glaze CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(storage PRIVATE glaze::glaze)
```

vcpkg, Conan, a system package or a library you built yourself can all provide `glaze`.
Switch the provider and none of your targets change.

## vcpkg in manifest mode {#sec-vcpkg}

With vcpkg, a `vcpkg.json` file in your repository lists the dependencies. The vcpkg
toolchain file installs them while CMake configures:

```{.json filename="CMakePresets.json (excerpt)"}
"toolchainFile": "${sourceDir}/external/vcpkg/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake"
```

What you get:

- **Pinned versions.** Pinning vcpkg itself, with a `builtin-baseline` commit or as a git
  submodule, fixes the version of every library.
- **Debug and release builds** of each library by default; a triplet can limit it to
  release, which halves build time.
- **Control per library.** *Triplets* decide how libraries are built (static or dynamic,
  which platform, which flags); *overlay ports* let you patch one.
- **A binary cache.** Each library is built once and reused by every later build and every
  project.
- **Every platform with one setup**, from Windows, macOS and Linux to Android and iOS.

The setup costs more than downloading a few libraries by hand, and the binary cache is what
pays it back. Once CI builds every change on every platform (@sec-ci), each run would
otherwise rebuild all dependencies from source. With the cache stored between runs, CI
rebuilds a library only when its version or its triplet changes, and each run spends its time
on your code.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `vcpkg.json`, `cmake/vcpkg-triplets/`, and vcpkg as a submodule in `external/vcpkg`

**Read more:** [vcpkg manifest mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/vcpkg/concepts/manifest-mode),
[triplets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/vcpkg/concepts/triplets)
:::

## Where Qt comes from {#sec-qt-source}

Qt is a dependency like any other, just a large one. You have two good options:

- **The [Qt Online Installer](https://www.qt.io/development/download-qt-installer-oss).**
  Ready in minutes. Point CMake at it with `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`.
- **Build Qt yourself**, from source or through your package manager. A full build takes
  hours, so build only the modules you use. In return, every flag and every dependency of Qt
  is under your control, on every platform.

::: {.more}
**Template:** the `dev` preset uses an installed Qt; the `qt-from-source` preset lets vcpkg build it
:::

## Reproducibility is control {#sec-reproducibility}

A cross-platform app runs on machines you have never seen. Each platform brings its own
surprises: Linux needs fontconfig, macOS frameworks, Windows the right runtime DLLs. Every
library linked dynamically must exist on the user's machine at run time.

The answer is control. When one tool builds every dependency the same way on every
platform, a build that works today still works tomorrow, on a colleague's machine, and in
CI. Prebuilt binaries from elsewhere bring flags and dependencies you did not choose.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
The more of your dependencies one tool builds for you, Qt included, the fewer surprises you
meet when you ship.
:::
